article_title: Three Pathways of Student-AI Interaction: Constraint-First Design for Higher-Order Thinking
citation: Zahra, F. T. (2025). Three Pathways of Student-AI Interaction: Constraint-First Design for Higher-Order Thinking. Manuscript under blind review; framework first presented at EAAI-25, Philadelphia, PA.
title: Next Level Teaching Blueprint (NLTB): three-stage constraint-first design for Strategic Dialogue
description: A replicable instructional design system with three sequenced stages and explicit interaction protocols, described by the article as having "a theoretical logic linking each element to Path 3 engagement." Stage 1 has students engage the problem fully without AI and document reasoning, securing epistemic agency and structurally preventing Paths 1 and 2. Stage 2 operationalizes Path 3 under explicit constraints: students share their Stage 1 reasoning, ask AI to challenge it, and probe responses; answers, summaries, and drafts are not permitted. Stage 3 requires metacognitive comparison of original versus AI-augmented thinking and construction of an integrated, evaluated position.
requirements: Assignments must be structured so that Path 1 and Path 2 responses are structurally non-compliant, and students must have their own documented position before AI contact
constraints: The article states formal evaluation of the campus-wide initiative is beyond the scope of the paper, and a controlled comparison of scaffolded and unscaffolded conditions remains to be run
examples: The NLTB was first implemented in the pilot research methods course, whose AI interaction protocols were derived from the developing framework; a campus-wide initiative funded at $22,100 across two phases involves six faculty across three colleges.
key_sources: Zahra, F. T. (2025). Three Pathways of Student-AI Interaction: Constraint-First Design for Higher-Order Thinking. Manuscript under blind review; framework first presented at EAAI-25, Philadelphia, PA. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00338

article_title: Natural Language Generation Using Deep Learning to Support MOOC Learners
citation: Chenglu Li & Wanli Xing. (2021). Natural Language Generation Using Deep Learning to Support MOOC Learners. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00235-x
title: Deep-learning NLG reply-generation pipeline (RNN and GPT-2) trained on MOOC forum post-reply pairs
description: A three-stage pipeline for generating forum replies: data preprocessing, model training, and quantitative evaluation. After cleaning (removing unreplied posts, stripping HTML, UTF-8 encoding, masking links), "there were 13,850 entries of post-reply pairs left", split 0.6/0.2/0.2 into training, validation, and testing sets. An LSTM-based RNN and a medium GPT-2 pretrained model (24 layers, 345 million parameters) were trained; generated replies were evaluated with word perplexity, Flesch-Kincaid grade level, and BERT-embedding cosine similarity against posts.
requirements: Posts paired with at least one human reply for supervised training
Sufficient computational power (the authors cite GPU limits in choosing the medium GPT-2 model)
constraints: Trained and evaluated on one creative thinking MOOC's forum data; web links are masked with a [LINK] token rather than generated
target_learning_goals: Automatic provision of supportive, contextually coherent replies to learner posts
examples: The testing set's 2770 posts were used as prompts, with model replies compared against original replies' readability and coherence metrics
key_sources: Chenglu Li & Wanli Xing. (2021). Natural Language Generation Using Deep Learning to Support MOOC Learners. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00235-x

article_title: Effects of High-Fidelity Simulation Training on Learning Outcomes and Satisfaction for Practising Registered Nurses: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Zhou Jie, Zhang Guowen, Song Peige, Liaw Sok Ying, Luk Tzu Tsun. (2026). Effects of High‐Fidelity Simulation Training on Learning Outcomes and Satisfaction for Practising Registered Nurses: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis. Journal of Clinical Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.70206
title: NLN Jeffries Simulation Theory outcome framework (knowledge, skills, self-confidence, satisfaction)
description: The review organises its outcome synthesis using the NLN Jeffries Simulation Theory framework, under which simulation learning outcomes are categorised into four types. As the review states, "Following the NLN Jeffries Simulation Theory framework, the outcomes were categorised as knowledge acquisition, professional skills, self‐confidence and learning satisfaction". Each category was separately meta-analysed, allowing effects, heterogeneity and study-design differences to be examined per outcome.
requirements: Outcome measures must be assignable to one of the four framework categories, with instruments identified per study.
constraints: The framework's four categories do not cover all potential learning outcomes; the review notes it could not examine outcomes such as clinical judgement and communication not reported in the reviewed studies.
examples: The review applied the framework to pool outcomes across eight studies, with data extracted including HFS design details (scenario, prebriefing, simulation and debriefing durations, manikin brand).
key_sources: Zhou Jie, Zhang Guowen, Song Peige, Liaw Sok Ying, Luk Tzu Tsun. (2026). Effects of High‐Fidelity Simulation Training on Learning Outcomes and Satisfaction for Practising Registered Nurses: A Systematic Review and Meta‐Analysis. Journal of Clinical Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.70206

article_title: Inclusive pedagogy in online simulation-based learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review.
citation: Langan, L., Frazer, K., Darley, A., Goodman, L., Browne, F., Fulfilled, P., Halligan, P., & Redmond, C. (2025). Inclusive pedagogy in online simulation‐based learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 81, 591–606. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16284
title: NLN Diversity and Inclusion Toolkit (2017)
description: The National League for Nursing (NLN) Diversity and Inclusion Toolkit (2017) is a source of grey literature identified in the review that "devotes a subsection to inclusive pedagogy in their toolkit". Whilst they do not explicitly define inclusive pedagogy, they affirm the need for pedagogical approaches that are theoretically appropriate, equitable, inclusive, and responsive to diverse perspectives. The toolkit provides specific questions for educators wanting to adopt inclusive pedagogy, which promotes the inclusion of student views.
requirements: The toolkit identifies specific key points applied to nursing that would benefit from further development.
target_learning_goals: equality, diversity and inclusion in nursing education
key_sources: Langan, L., Frazer, K., Darley, A., Goodman, L., Browne, F., Fulfilled, P., Halligan, P., & Redmond, C. (2025). Inclusive pedagogy in online simulation‐based learning in undergraduate nursing education: A scoping review. Journal of Advanced Nursing, 81, 591–606. https://doi.org/10.1111/jan.16284

article_title: Virtual simulation scenario for teaching standard precautions: a validation study.
citation: Gusmão Cristine Maria Pereira, Lima Laís do Espirito Santo, Menegueti Mayra Gonçalves, Zamarioli Cristina Mara, Gir Elucir, Reis Renata Karina. (2026). Virtual simulation scenario for teaching standard precautions: a validation study. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2025-0346
title: Scenario structure based on NLN/Jeffries Simulation Theory and INACSL Healthcare Simulation Standards of Best Practice
description: The article structures the virtual simulation scenario on two reference frameworks: the National League for Nursing/Jeffries Simulation Theory (NLN/JST) and the Healthcare Simulation Standards of Best Practice™ of the International Nursing Association for Clinical Simulation and Learning (INACSL). The authors state that "The scenario structure was based on the National League for Nursing/Jeffries Simulation Theory (NLN/JST) and the Healthcare Simulation Standards of Best Practice™", with technical content grounded in current evidence and guidelines on Standard Precautions and PPE use. They attribute the high ratings for items such as 'target audience' and 'objectives' to this structure.
requirements: Rigorous planning and validation to ensure alignment with the learning objectives, per the frameworks the article cites
examples: The development flowchart proceeds from defining the scenario title and target audience through searching and selecting content, developing prebriefing, briefing, debriefing, checklist, and scoring, to review and validation
key_sources: Gusmão Cristine Maria Pereira, Lima Laís do Espirito Santo, Menegueti Mayra Gonçalves, Zamarioli Cristina Mara, Gir Elucir, Reis Renata Karina. (2026). Virtual simulation scenario for teaching standard precautions: a validation study. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2025-0346

article_title: Factors associated with nursing students' satisfaction with simulation-based assessments: interaction between psychological safety and gender in a cross-sectional study.
citation: Kyung Minjung, Kim Hieun, Kim Jung-Hee. (2025). Factors associated with nursing students’ satisfaction with simulation-based assessments: interaction between psychological safety and gender in a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07648-z
title: NLN/Jeffries Simulation Framework as organizing model for satisfaction in simulation-based assessment
description: The study structures its survey and analysis around the NLN/Jeffries Simulation Framework, which "includes five components: participant, facilitator, educational practices, simulation design characteristics, and outcomes". The authors operationalized participant characteristics, psychological safety as an educational-practice variable, and satisfaction as the outcome, omitting the facilitator component because all students experienced the same learning conditions. In the framework, "simulation design is identified as one of the key factors contributing to ideal simulation experiences for nursing students".
requirements: All students experience comparable learning conditions for the facilitator component to be omitted from assessment
constraints: The facilitator component was not assessed in this study
examples: The 54-item course-evaluation survey selected variables based on the framework's components
key_sources: Kyung Minjung, Kim Hieun, Kim Jung-Hee. (2025). Factors associated with nursing students’ satisfaction with simulation-based assessments: interaction between psychological safety and gender in a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07648-z

article_title: Optimising Educational Practices in Simulation-Based Nursing Education: Results of A National Survey.
citation: Alsadi, M., Alosta, M. R., Othman, E. H., Obiedallah, H., & Nashwan, A. J. (2025). Optimising Educational Practices in Simulation‐Based Nursing Education: Results of A National Survey. Nursing Open, 12(4), e70172. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70172
title: NLN/Jeffries framework describing simulation design dimensions and educational practices
description: The article applies the National League for Nursing (NLN) framework developed by Jeffries, which "underscores the specific features in simulation design and implementation of best educational practices to evaluate and conclude simulation‐based learning in undergraduate nursing education." It is operationalised through two instruments: the 20-item Simulation Design Scale, covering "objectives," "support," "problem‐solving," "feedback," and "fidelity," and the 16-item Educational Practices Questionnaire covering "active learning," "collaboration," "diverse ways of learning," and "expectations." The framework "has been developed based on theoretical and empirical literature to guide the development and assessment of learning processes."
requirements: Simulation implementation must be based on pedagogical principles and well-defined educational practices, per the article citing Jeffries (2005)
constraints: The article notes limited studies guide designing, implementing, and evaluating simulations in nursing
target_learning_goals: bridging theory and practice in simulation-based education
examples: The national survey administered the SDS and EPQ to 966 Jordanian nursing students to evaluate simulation designs and associated educational practices
key_sources: Alsadi, M., Alosta, M. R., Othman, E. H., Obiedallah, H., & Nashwan, A. J. (2025). Optimising Educational Practices in Simulation‐Based Nursing Education: Results of A National Survey. Nursing Open, 12(4), e70172. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70172

article_title: Clinical simulation scenarios for the planning and management of infusion therapy by nurses.
citation: Meszaros Mariana de Jesus; de Almeida Angélica Olivetto; da Silva Ruana Luiz Ferreira; Eduardo Aline Helena Appoloni; Lima Maria Helena de Melo; Oliveira-Kumakura Ana Railka de Souza. (2023). Clinical simulation scenarios for the planning and management of infusion therapy by nurses. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2023-0019
title: NLN Jeffries Simulation Theory four-step scenario structure (pre-briefing, briefing, scenario, debriefing)
description: The article structures its scenarios on the NLN Jeffries Simulation Theory and INACSL guidelines, which conceptualize simulation-based teaching through "the following elements: the facilitator, the student, educational practices, simulation design (which includes objectives, fidelity, support for the participant , problem solving and debriefing) and learning outcomes." For elaboration, four steps were considered: pre-briefing presenting the simulated environment and resources, briefing with vignettes containing sufficient clinical-case data, the clinical simulation scenario itself, and debriefing in which participants reflect on the simulated experience with a facilitator.
requirements: A facilitator, defined objectives, fidelity, participant support, problem solving and a debriefing phase guided by a theoretical reference
constraints: Applied in the article to nursing education for infusion therapy with high-fidelity simulation
target_learners: Nurses and nursing students in continuing or undergraduate education
target_learning_goals: Clinical judgment, decision-making and safe infusion therapy management
examples: The study's scenarios followed pre-briefing, briefing, the 15-minute simulated scenario, and formative debriefing during the experience plus 30-minute summative debriefing afterwards
key_sources: Meszaros Mariana de Jesus; de Almeida Angélica Olivetto; da Silva Ruana Luiz Ferreira; Eduardo Aline Helena Appoloni; Lima Maria Helena de Melo; Oliveira-Kumakura Ana Railka de Souza. (2023). Clinical simulation scenarios for the planning and management of infusion therapy by nurses. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2023-0019
